source_doc: Exercises/Build_an_Interactive_Dashboard.docx > Instructions, Part 1 and Part 2 steps 7-8 (S6 test take)

ide.notes: Off camera, before OBS starts: VS Code saves open editors and folder expansion in the codespace, so the previous take's state (data expanded, the CSV open) is reset first. The Claude Code panel reopens its last session, so prepare clicks New session (and returns to Chat).

narration.text: I'll start at github.com/codespaces. A codespace is a complete development workspace that runs in your browser, so there's nothing to install.
On the left, under By repository, I'll click my repository, my-agentic-workshop. As you can see, the list narrows to that repository's codespaces.

steps.notes: Matched by repository id: by name, my-agentic-workshop is a prefix of every take repo (take02 of S6 clicked take06's link, 2026-10-07).

narration.text: Then I'll click my codespace. GitHub gives every codespace a random two-word name. This one is called {codespace_display}. Yours will have a different name.

steps.notes: Opens in a new tab (the link has target=_blank). Codespaces occasionally stalls on 'Setting up your codespace'; the runner reloads once after 90 s. A stopped codespace takes about a minute to start; that wait is cut in the edit.

narration.text: A box asks whether I trust the authors of the files in this folder. It's my own repository, so I'll click Trust Folder & Continue.

steps.notes: Appears only on a codespace's first open. The take's existing codespace is already trusted, so this step is skipped there; a fresh take repo shows it.

narration.text: The file list isn't showing, so I'll click the Explorer icon at the top of the bar on the far left.

steps.notes: Clicking Explorer while it is open would close it, so the step runs only when the file list is hidden.

narration.text: The Explorer, on the left, lists the files in the repository. I'll open the data folder,

steps.notes: A click on an expanded folder collapses it, so the take stops if data is already open (prepare resets it).

narration.text: and select monthlysummary.csv. The first line lists the columns, from location and airport code to delays, cancellations and taxi times. Each row after that is one airport in one month, about twenty-four thousand rows in all.
A notice offers to install the Rainbow CSV extension. We won't need it, so I'll close it with the X.
Claude Code lives in the panel on the right-hand side of the screen. I'll click the Claude Code tab.

steps.notes: When the codespace already shows a Claude Code tab next to Chat: after a restart it does (take06, 2026-10-07). On a codespace's very first open it doesn't, so p2.07b and c run instead.

narration.text: Claude Code lives in the panel on the right-hand side of the screen. As of this writing, a new codespace doesn't show a Claude Code tab, so I'll click the three dots next to Chat,
and choose Claude Code. Notice that the Chat tab next to it is GitHub Copilot, a different assistant. We're using Claude Code in this video.
Claude Code opens with two welcome cards. We won't need them, so I'll close Learn Claude Code with its X,

steps.notes: The doc's welcome cards, shown once Claude Code is logged in (take06, 2026-10-07): 'Learn Claude Code' closes with its Hide onboarding X; 'Auto mode is now Claude Code's default permission mode.' with its Close X.

narration.text: and then Auto mode.

steps.notes: The doc's welcome cards, shown once Claude Code is logged in (take06, 2026-10-07): 'Learn Claude Code' closes with its Hide onboarding X; 'Auto mode is now Claude Code's default permission mode.' with its Close X.

narration.text: This codespace already has an earlier conversation, so I'll click New session to start fresh.

steps.notes: Only in a reused codespace: the panel reopens its last conversation (with any open question form) after a reconnect, and an off-camera New session does not survive it (s7_take05). A fresh repo skips this step.

action.text:
Before we build anything, add two rules to CLAUDE.md:
- Keep this file short. When we finish a piece of work, write notes about it in a file in the docs folder, and add a one-line pointer to that file here.
- When I ask you to commit, commit to the main branch and push it to GitHub. Don't create other branches.

narration.text: Before we build anything, I'll give Claude two standing rules. I'll enter this prompt. Every prompt in this video is available via the description.

steps.notes: Typed at natural speed, not pasted (R67): the edit speeds the typing up or cuts its middle, so the line plays over the finished prompt. The description carries every prompt.

narration.text: These rules go in CLAUDE.md, a file that Claude reads at the start of every session, so they apply from now on.
The first rule keeps that file short. On a long project, notes pile up, and Claude would read all of them every time.
The second rule keeps our work on the main branch, which GitHub shows on the repository's front page. Without it, Claude may save the work on a separate branch.
I'll click the send arrow. As you can see, the prompt moves into the conversation.

steps.notes: Send arrow confirmed in take06 (2026-10-07). The busy panel shows 'Queue another message'.

narration.text: Claude checks CLAUDE.md and finds both rules already there, so it makes no changes.
points: Claude's reply: it added both rules to CLAUDE.md (doc step 9).
If the reply shows the edit, point at the two new lines.

steps.notes: Usually under 20 s: real time with the cut rules (R39). Auto mode edits CLAUDE.md without a prompt. Marks (R75): the Read row and the reply's first sentence, by OCR of the panel; the reply is on screen before the wait ends (take06).

action.text: I have a CSV of U.S. flight data. Build me a single interactive dashboard for an aviation operations team. Use data visualization best practices. Create calculated fields, filters, and parameters where they make sense. Don't limit yourself to just what's in the data; apply what you know about the airline industry and current trends to decide what's useful. Visuals should interact with each other where appropriate. Before you start building, tell me what options we have and ask any questions you need answered. Note that I want the dashboard to run here in my Codespace so I can open it in my browser. The file is at: data/monthlysummary.csv

narration.text: Now let's ask for the dashboard. I'll enter the dashboard prompt.

steps.notes: Typed at natural speed, not pasted (R67): the edit speeds the typing up or cuts its middle, so the line plays over the finished prompt. The description carries every prompt.

narration.text: Notice what the prompt describes: the audience, an aviation operations team, and the quality bar, data visualization best practices.

overlay.title: The dashboard prompt

steps.notes: The long prompt scrolls inside the message box (take06, 2:26), so the whole prompt is shown on an overlay and the highlights go on it (R77). The overlay stays up through p2.10d.

narration.text: It doesn't name a chart type, a column, or a framework. It also tells Claude to look beyond the data, and apply what it knows about the airline industry.

target.match: Don't limit yourself to just what's in the data; apply what you know about the airline industry

narration.text: Note that we ask for options before Claude builds anything. This is a best practice. Claude lays out the choices, and we make the decisions that matter.

target.match: Before you start building, tell me what options we have and ask any questions you need answered

narration.text: I'll click the send arrow. Claude starts by reading the data.

steps.notes: Send arrow confirmed in take06 (2026-10-07). The busy panel shows 'Queue another message'.

narration.text: In this case, it counts the rows, reads the columns, and checks the other files in the data folder before it proposes anything. Then it writes up what it found.
points: Claude reads the CSV first, to learn the columns, before it proposes anything.

steps.notes: p2.10e already says Claude starts by reading the data (take06 had both, 3:00 and 3:03). The 20 s of tool calls are time-lapsed under this line (realtime_max_s 10 for this step) instead of cut, so the viewer sees the reading happen (R75).

narration.text: Claude lays out what it found and what it could build. In this run, it offers three layouts and recommends one page of linked charts. Key numbers run across the top, then a map of airports, a trend line and a ranking; a click on one chart filters the others. It also flags things to check, such as cancellation counts that look low, and the 2020 drop in flights, which would dominate any trend. Treat findings like these as things to check, not facts. Another run may suggest different charts, but the shape of the reply is what to expect: findings, options, and questions.
points: Claude laid out the options: name the frameworks it offered and the one it recommends.
Its plan for the page (charts, filters, parameters) in one sentence.
Arrive on its questions ("Questions for you" in the doc's run); read one or two aloud, e.g. cancellations or alert thresholds.
Any data quirks it found on its own (doc's run: missing coordinates, territories): findings to verify, not facts.

steps.notes: Reading a reply on camera (S7): the runner jumps the conversation to the start of Claude's last reply, below the pinned prompt, holds, then scrolls through it at a steady reading pace (runner READ_PX_S) and holds. The narration is written after the run (R33); the edit fits the scroll to it. The narrow panel at 2x shows too little of the reply to follow (take06, 3:17), so its main points go on an overlay, worded as what Claude may suggest (R76, R77); the scroll keeps playing beside it. Round 2 (David, 2026-10-07): the last item said the questions, one level below its sentence; it now sums up the shape of the reply and appears on 'findings' (R80; his Premiere edit moved it there).

items.text: Findings: 23,878 rows, 378 airports, Jan 2020 to Sep 2025
Three layouts: a one-page command center (its pick), an airport deep-dive, or two tabs
Linked charts: key numbers, a map, a trend line, a ranking; a click filters the rest
Things to check: cancellation counts look low; the 2020 drop would dominate a trend
Shape of the reply: findings, options, and questions

narration.text: This time, Claude asks its questions in a form, starting with the layout. I could answer each one here, but instead I'll press Escape to close the form, and answer in my own words.

steps.notes: Runs between p3.11a and p3.11b (lettered e because the others were taken). Only when Claude asks with its question form (s7_take04) instead of plain text (s7_take01, take02). Escape closes the form ('Tool interrupted') and the message box takes the scripted answer (p3.11b). Checked off camera on take08, 2026-10-07. Mark (R75): the whole form, from its first question to 'Esc to cancel' (OCR span). R78: the questions clause is said before Escape. Round 2 (David, 2026-10-07): only the layout question is readable; the others sit behind tabs cut to 'La… E… C… Aud…', so the line no longer names them (R81).

action.text: Let's use Plotly Dash. Go with your defaults for everything else.

narration.text: In the box at the bottom, I'll type my answer. We'll use Plotly Dash, a Python framework for interactive web dashboards, and let Claude go with its defaults for everything else.

steps.notes: Edited 2026-10-07 after David's review of s7_take06 (docs/S7_FIX_PLAN.md): R78, the form is closed by now, so 'I could answer each of Claude's questions' moved into p3.11e. Was approved; needs David's OK.

narration.text: I'll click the send arrow, and Claude starts building.

steps.notes: Send arrow confirmed in take06 (2026-10-07). The busy panel shows 'Queue another message'.

narration.text: That's the direction prompt at work. We set the goal and made the decision that mattered most, and Claude handles the implementation.

steps.notes: Plays over the first seconds of the build (live footage). Calls back to the opening (p0.03).

narration.text: Claude starts the build. In this case, it first loads a skill called dataviz: a packaged set of instructions that Claude loads only when a task calls for it. We didn't ask for it; Claude judged it relevant. From here, Claude may install tools, or write and run code, to do its work. This build took about three minutes.
points: Title card "Claude is building: about N minutes", then a 6 to 10 s time-lapse (R39).
If Claude loads a skill (such as dataviz): a skill is a packaged set of instructions that Claude loads only when a task calls for it. You didn't ask for it; Claude judged it relevant.
If it hits an error, it explains it and fixes it on its own (at 1x only if David picks the moment, R39).
New files, such as app.py and an assets folder, appear in the Explorer. The U means new, and not yet saved to GitHub.
Dash, Plotly and pandas were already installed in the codespace, so Claude didn't need to install them.
"Allow this bash command?" to restart the dashboard with pkill: routine, click Yes (1x, a visible click, R39, R47). Auto mode lets Claude edit and run commands, and asks before it stops a program.
Claude's summary says it ran and tested the code but couldn't see the page: sets up Part 5.

steps.notes: About 7 min in the workshop walk-through; 3.8 min in take06. The dataviz skill row is on screen as the build starts (take06, 4:28), so it is named and marked during 9 s at 1x before the card (before_card_s). The rest of the build is the card and the lapse. app.py and the summary are p4.12b, after the result. Autopilot: routine prompts approved, RISKY ones stop the take.

narration.text: When Claude is done, a new file, app.py, appears in the Explorer. The U means it's new, and not yet saved to GitHub. But note that in our case, the dashboard isn't displaying: nothing opened in the browser.

steps.notes: A line-only step (after: p4.12): it rides on the footage after the build's result, consuming no footage of its own; the next step's bridge shows the picture under it. 'tests it' dropped (not visible, R75); 'in our case' (R76); David's wording for the lead-in to Ports. Round 3 (2026-10-07): 'Claude also reports that the dashboard is running' dropped: the report had scrolled out of the panel and the camera was on the Explorer (R81); back to draft for David's OK.

narration.text: If it looks like Claude is done and you don't see the dashboard, check the browser tabs. If it isn't there, it's still running inside the codespace, on port 8050, and you can open it from the panel below the editor. Next to Terminal, I'll click the Ports tab.

steps.notes: R74: Codespaces opens the dashboard on its own (the template's onAutoForward: openBrowser) or not; the runner closes any tab that opens by itself, so the take always shows the Ports route. The bottom panel must be open for the Ports tab to show. Edited 2026-10-07 after David's review of s7_take06 (docs/S7_FIX_PLAN.md): David's wording ('check the browser tabs, or click the Ports tab next to the Terminal tab'); the tab strip is marked (full frame while it shows, R40). Was approved; needs David's OK.

narration.text: Port 8050 is listed here. I'll hover over its row,

steps.notes: Hover on the port's name (the row's centre is Running Process, which shows a tooltip). The globe is a.codicon-ports-open-browser-icon, aria-label 'Open in Browser' (s7_take02, 2026-10-07).

narration.text: and click the globe icon. As you can see, the dashboard opens in a new tab.

steps.notes: Opens the -8050.app.github.dev tab; the camera zooms out on the cut (R44) and holds full frame on the address (R40).

narration.text: Note the address, which ends in 8050.app.github.dev. Codespaces checks that you're signed in to GitHub before it shows the page, so by default, only you can open it.
